title: Social Responsibility of Business and Business Ethics
tagline: What society is entitled to expect of a firm, the arguments for and against that claim, and the ethical principles that govern conduct. Unit weight: 5 marks.

overview.intro: A business operates on a licence granted by society: it uses common resources, employs people, draws on the education and infrastructure others pay for, and sells to customers who trust its claims. That licence carries an obligation. This five-mark unit sets out what social responsibility means, who the parties are that a firm answers to, the arguments on both sides of the question, and the case against the claim. It then defines business ethics, the factors that shape ethical behaviour in a firm, and the practical codes through which ethics becomes something more than a statement on a wall.

facts.label: Stakeholders owed responsibility
facts.value: Shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, community and the state.

facts.label: Ethics vs law
facts.value: Law states the minimum that must be done; ethics governs what ought to be done beyond it.

facts.label: Two views
facts.value: The economic view holds that profit is the only duty; the socio-economic view holds that profit must be earned within social limits.

learningOutcomes: Identify the parties to whom a business is responsible.
Explain the arguments for and against social responsibility.
Define business ethics and state the factors affecting it.
Describe how a firm institutionalises ethical conduct.

learn.title: Meaning and stakeholders of social responsibility

blocks.text: Social responsibility of business is the obligation of an enterprise to act in a way that benefits society as a whole alongside its own owners, rather than pursuing profit without regard for the consequences of its conduct. It rests on the observation that a firm consumes social resources, employs people, and affects the air, water and neighbourhood around it, so part of the cost of its activity is borne by people who never signed a contract with it. Responsibility therefore extends beyond the customer to every stakeholder.

blocks.caption: Social responsibility towards each stakeholder
rows: Shareholders
Honest reporting, lawful conduct, sustainable rather than short-term profit
Employees
Fair wages, safe conditions, equality of opportunity and training
Customers
Quality goods at fair prices, honest advertising, after-sales redress
Suppliers
Fair terms and prompt payment rather than squeezing the weaker party
Community
Environmental care, local employment, support for civic life
The state
Payment of taxes, compliance with law, no corruption

items.text: A plant treating its effluent instead of discharging it into the river.
items.note: The community bears the cost of untreated waste, so treating it is responsibility rather than generosity.

items.text: A firm publishing accurate product labelling even when the claim would pass unnoticed.
items.note: Responsibility towards customers is met through honesty rather than through legal minimum compliance alone.

learn.title: Arguments for and against social responsibility

blocks.text: The arguments for social responsibility are that business uses social resources and should therefore return something to society; that responsible conduct builds the reputation and goodwill that later become revenue; that it pre-empts government regulation by showing that the industry can govern itself; and that responsible use of resources is simply the condition of the business continuing to exist. The arguments against are that the only social duty of business is to maximise profit for its owners, that the cost of social action is ultimately passed to customers in higher prices, that business already pays society through taxes, and that managers are not qualified or elected to decide what society needs.

blocks.caption: The case for and the case against
rows: Business draws on social resources and should return value
Profit maximisation is the sole duty to shareholders
Goodwill and reputation convert into long-run revenue
Social cost is passed on as higher prices to consumers
Voluntary action reduces the pressure for regulation
Business already contributes through taxation
Ethical conduct protects the licence to operate
Managers have no mandate to decide social priorities

blocks.text: The resolution accepted in modern practice is the socio-economic view: profit remains the economic purpose, but it must be earned within limits set by law, ethics and the interest of other stakeholders. A firm that treats responsibility as a cost centre tends to lose the argument eventually, because the consequences it ignored arrive as regulation, litigation or an exodus of customers and staff.

learn.title: Business ethics: meaning and the factors that shape it

blocks.text: Business ethics is the set of moral principles and standards that guide the conduct of business and distinguish right from wrong in commercial behaviour. Ethics goes where law stops: the law states the minimum that must be done and fixes a penalty for failing, while ethics governs what ought to be done and is enforced by reputation and conscience. Unethical conduct is not always illegal, and some legal conduct is still unethical, which is exactly why firms need a code rather than only a compliance manual.

items.meaning: Moral principles and standards that govern acceptable conduct in business.
Written statement of the standards a firm expects its people to observe.
Situation in which a person’s private gain competes with her duty to the firm.
Reporting of unethical or illegal conduct within the organisation to those who can act.

blocks.caption: Factors affecting the ethical behaviour of a firm
rows: Leadership
What the top management tolerates becomes the real policy
Individual values
Personal upbringing and conviction of each employee
Organisational culture
Whether the firm rewards results only or results by proper means
Code and training
Whether standards are written, taught and discussed
External environment
Laws, public scrutiny and the practice of competitors

items: A written code stating the standards expected in each area of conduct.
Ethics training at induction and periodically thereafter.
An anonymous channel for raising concerns without fear.
Consistent consequences when a code is breached, at every level of seniority.
Top management visibly observing the same standards it sets.

blocks.text: A code becomes effective only when it changes decisions. The practical steps are to embed ethics into hiring and appraisal, so that conduct is assessed alongside output; to give employees a safe route for reporting concerns, since most misconduct is first noticed by a junior person who has the least power; to investigate reports promptly and consistently; and to apply consequences without exception, because a single unenforced breach teaches everyone that the code is decoration. Periodic review of the code against actual cases keeps it alive rather than aspirational.

items.text: A procurement manager whose relative owns a supplier firm.
items.note: A conflict of interest is managed by disclosure and withdrawal from the decision, which is what the code should require in advance.

items.text: A junior accountant reporting an instruction to misstate a figure.
items.note: Whistle-blowing needs protection built into policy, since the reporter has almost everything to lose.

labels: Law: the minimum, enforced by penalty
Ethics: the standard beyond law, enforced by code and conscience
Reputation: the market’s verdict, enforced by customers and staff
Conduct can be legal yet still breach the outer two rings

keyPoints: Social responsibility is the obligation to benefit society alongside owners.
It is owed to shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, community and the state.
For: use of social resources, goodwill, pre-emption of regulation and protection of the licence to operate.
Against: profit is the only duty, costs are passed on, taxes already are the contribution, managers have no mandate.
The socio-economic view holds that profit must be earned within social limits.
Business ethics is the set of moral principles distinguishing right from wrong in commerce.
Law is the minimum enforceable standard; ethics governs what ought to be done.
Ethics are shaped by leadership, individual values, culture, code and training, and the external environment.
A code works only when it is trained, reported through safely, and enforced consistently.
Conflicts of interest are managed by disclosure and withdrawal from the decision.
examFocus: Five marks means concise: give the definition, four stakeholders with one line each, and a balanced pair of arguments.
Ethics answers gain by contrasting with law explicitly, since that contrast is the usual distinguishing mark.
For factors affecting ethics, name the factor and its effect rather than listing bare headings.

vocabulary.meaning: Obligation of business to act for the benefit of society alongside its owners.
Moral principles and standards guiding acceptable conduct in business.
Position that profit must be earned within limits set by society and law.
Written statement of the standards a firm requires its people to observe.
Situation where private gain competes with duty to the firm.
Reporting of misconduct inside the organisation to those able to act on it.
Reputation value built by consistent conduct, which converts into future revenue.

options: Obligation to act for the benefit of society alongside owners
Strict obedience to the law only
Donating a fixed percentage of profit every year
questions.answer: Obligation to act for the benefit of society alongside owners
questions.explanation: Responsibility covers the whole set of stakeholders and the consequences of the firm’s conduct, not merely one obligation such as tax or charity.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an argument AGAINST social responsibility?
options: The cost is ultimately passed to consumers in higher prices
It protects the licence to operate
questions.answer: The cost is ultimately passed to consumers in higher prices
questions.explanation: The cost argument holds that social spending is recovered from customers, while the other three are arguments in favour.

questions.prompt: The difference between law and ethics is that:
options: Law is enforced by penalty, ethics by code, conscience and reputation
Ethics is compulsory and law is optional
Both are enforced only by the state
Ethics applies only to listed companies
questions.answer: Law is enforced by penalty, ethics by code, conscience and reputation
questions.explanation: Law fixes the enforceable minimum with penalties behind it, while ethics governs conduct beyond that minimum through internal and social enforcement.

questions.prompt: The strongest single influence on the ethical conduct of a firm is:
options: The size of its advertising budget
The behaviour its top management tolerates
The number of policies it publishes
questions.answer: The behaviour its top management tolerates
questions.explanation: Culture follows what leadership rewards and tolerates, so conduct at the top sets the real standard regardless of what the code says.

questions.prompt: The written statement of the standards of conduct a firm expects its employees to observe is called a code of __________ .
questions.explanation: The code converts general expectations into stated standards that can be taught, referred to and enforced.

questions.prompt: The reporting of unethical or illegal conduct within an organisation by a person who works there is known as whistle- __________ .
questions.explanation: Blowing the whistle is how misconduct first noticed by a junior employee reaches those able to act on it.

questions.prompt: State four arguments in favour of social responsibility.
questions.answer: Four arguments are: business draws on social resources such as infrastructure and educated labour and should return value in exchange; responsible conduct builds reputation and goodwill that convert into long-run revenue; voluntary responsibility reduces the pressure for government regulation of the industry; and responsible use of the environment protects the licence to operate. Ethical conduct also avoids litigation and staff turnover.
questions.explanation: Each argument needs a line of reasoning, because asserting the duty without explaining why earns only half marks.

questions.prompt: Mention four factors that affect the ethical behaviour of a firm.
questions.answer: Four factors are: the example set by top management, since what leaders tolerate becomes the real policy; the personal values of individual employees; the organisational culture, which decides whether results alone or results by proper means are rewarded; and the written code together with the training that supports it. The external environment of laws, public scrutiny and competitors’ practice also shapes conduct.
questions.explanation: Factors must be named with their effect, since the effect is what carries the marks.

questions.prompt: Explain the arguments for and against social responsibility and state which view is accepted in practice.
questions.answer: The arguments for are that business consumes social resources and should give back; that responsible conduct builds goodwill and reputation which later produce revenue; that voluntary action pre-empts restrictive regulation; and that ethical use of resources is the condition of continued operation. The arguments against are that the only duty of business is to maximise profit for its owners, that social spending is recovered from customers in higher prices, that business already contributes through taxation, and that managers have neither the qualification nor the mandate to decide society’s needs. The accepted position is the socio-economic view: profit remains the economic purpose of the enterprise but must be earned within limits set by law, ethics and the legitimate interests of other stakeholders, because the consequences of ignoring those limits return as regulation, litigation and loss of customers and staff.
questions.explanation: Full marks need both sides stated fairly and then a reasoned preference rather than an unsupported assertion.

questions.prompt: A cosmetic firm is found to have tested a product line on animals in a country where the practice is legal but widely condemned, and its advertising omits a known side effect. Classify both incidents under law and ethics, and state what the firm should do.
questions.answer: The animal testing is legal where it was carried out, so it does not breach law, but it breaches the ethical expectations of customers and staff who now judge the firm by a standard beyond legality. The omission of a known side effect is both unethical and, in most consumer markets, unlawful, since advertising must not mislead or conceal material risk. The firm should withdraw and correct the advertisement without delay, disclose the side effect in all packaging and marketing, review whether the testing can be replaced by approved alternatives, and state its position openly rather than denying it. It should also add both cases to its code of conduct so that the standard applies prospectively. The lesson is that legality is the floor, and a firm judged only by that floor loses the two outer controls, ethics and reputation, which are precisely the ones customers enforce.
questions.explanation: Marks depend on separating the two incidents correctly, noting that one is legal but unethical while the other is both, and prescribing actions rather than merely condemning.
